holidays.name: Slay a Dragon Day
holidays.description: Dust off your imaginary sword and shield. This is the day to face down your own personal dragons, whether that's a towering to-do list, a scary email, or an actual fire-breathing lizard if you have one handy. It falls on the same day as St. George's Day, so expect plenty of dragon-themed fun, banners, and storytelling.
holidays.origin: The day shares its date with St. George's Day, which marks the anniversary of the death of Saint George. He was a Roman soldier who, according to legend, saved a king's daughter by slaying a dragon. The dragon-slaying tale grew into one of Europe's best-loved legends, and the date became a playful excuse to celebrate dragon-fighting.
holidays.funFact: Saint George was reportedly born in Cappadocia, in what is now Turkey. The dragon story only became attached to him in medieval times, long after his death.

holidays.name: Movie Theatre Day
holidays.description: A day to celebrate the big screen, the sticky floors, the giant tubs of popcorn and the hush that falls when the lights go down. Grab a ticket, claim your favorite seat and enjoy a film the way it was meant to be seen: with strangers, snacks and a very large screen.
holidays.origin: It's an unofficial observance with no documented founder. The date lines up with April 23, 1896, when Thomas Edison's Vitascope projected films for a paying audience at Koster and Bial's Music Hall in New York City. Many film historians consider that show the birth of the American movie theater.
holidays.funFact: That first movie-house screening in 1896 used a screen about 20 feet wide by 12 feet tall, and audiences were amazed by the short films shown on it.

holidays.name: National Talk Like Shakespeare Day
holidays.description: Thou art hereby encouraged to swap everyday chatter for the flowery speech of the Bard. Greet coworkers with a hearty "good morrow," call your friends "knaves," and deliver your lunch order in iambic pentameter. Verily, it is glorious nonsense.
holidays.origin: The day falls on April 23, traditionally linked to the death of William Shakespeare in 1616 and often to his birth in 1564 as well. It became an official observance in Illinois when Governor Pat Quinn proclaimed it.
holidays.funFact: Shakespeare wrote about 39 plays and 154 sonnets, and he is credited with inventing or popularizing many words and phrases we still use today.
